title: Could Humans Really Live on Mars? The Honest Answer
description:
Mars is the most Earth-like planet we can reach, and it would still try to kill you in a dozen different ways. We walk through every problem a Mars settler would face, from the air and the cold to radiation and toxic dirt, and what NASA's robots have already learned about solving them.

scenes.narration: Mars is the most Earth-like world we can reach. It would still try to kill you in at least six different ways.
scenes.headline: COULD YOU LIVE ON MARS?

visual.note: full globe of Mars showing the great canyon

scenes.narration: On paper, Mars looks promising. A day there lasts about twenty-four point six hours, almost exactly like ours. It has seasons, polar ice caps, and mountains. Robots have been driving across it for decades. So picture yourself stepping out of a lander. Let's go through the problems, one at a time.
scenes.headline: ON PAPER, PROMISING

visual.note: Perseverance rover selfie on the Martian surface

scenes.narration: Problem zero is getting there. Earth and Mars line up for an efficient trip only about once every twenty-six months. Miss the window and you wait more than two years. Even then, the journey takes around seven months, and the Perseverance rover's curving path covered about three hundred fourteen million miles.
scenes.headline: A WINDOW EVERY 26 MONTHS

visual.note: Atlas V rocket launching the Mars 2020 mission

scenes.narration: And once you land, home is far away. Depending on where the two planets are in their orbits, a radio message takes somewhere between about three and twenty-two minutes to cross the gap, one way. You can't have a conversation with Earth. In an emergency, you are on your own.
scenes.headline: 22 MINUTES TO SAY HELLO

visual.note: giant Deep Space Network dish antenna

scenes.narration: Problem one: the air. Take a breath on Mars and you'd get almost entirely carbon dioxide, about ninety-five percent. Oxygen makes up less than a fifth of one percent. And there's very little air at all.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM ONE: THE AIR

visual.note: thin haze of the Martian atmosphere along the horizon

scenes.narration: Problem two is closely related: pressure. The air on Mars presses down with only about six tenths of one percent of the pressure at sea level on Earth. That's far thinner than the air at the top of Mount Everest, and thin enough to matter in a frightening way.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM TWO: PRESSURE

visual.note: wide Martian landscape under a pale sky

scenes.narration: At that pressure, water boils at a temperature far below that of your body. Without a pressure suit, the moisture on your tongue and in your eyes would start boiling away within seconds. You would black out quickly. On Mars, a spacesuit isn't gear. It's your atmosphere.
scenes.headline: WHERE YOUR SPIT BOILS

visual.note: prototype planetary exploration spacesuit

scenes.narration: Problem three: the cold. The average temperature on Mars is around minus seventy-four degrees Fahrenheit. Near the poles, nights can plunge to about minus two hundred twenty-five. On a perfect summer day at the equator, it can reach about seventy degrees.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM THREE: THE COLD

visual.note: Martian north polar ice cap

scenes.narration: But here's the weird part. The air is so thin it can't hold heat. Stand at the equator at noon, and NASA says your feet might feel like a spring day, around seventy-five degrees, while the air at your head is close to freezing.
scenes.headline: WARM FEET, FREEZING HEAD
scenes.sub: 24°C at your feet, 0°C at your head

visual.spec: Standing astronaut silhouette on Mars with a temperature scale: about 75 degrees Fahrenheit at the feet near the ground and about 32 degrees Fahrenheit at head height

scenes.narration: Problem four is the one you can't see or feel: radiation. Earth wraps you in a thick atmosphere and a global magnetic field that deflects charged particles from space. Mars has neither. It lost its global magnetic field long ago, and it has only about one percent as much atmosphere as Earth.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM FOUR: RADIATION

visual.query: MAVEN solar wind stripping Mars atmosphere
visual.note: illustration of the solar wind stripping the Martian atmosphere

scenes.narration: NASA's Curiosity rover carries a radiation detector, and it measured the dose at the surface. It averaged about two thirds of a millisievert per day. That's roughly like getting thirty chest X-rays every single day, just by standing outside.
scenes.headline: THIRTY X-RAYS A DAY

visual.query: Curiosity rover RAD radiation assessment detector
visual.note: Curiosity rover on Mars

scenes.narration: Add up the flight there, the stay, and the trip home, and a mission could total around one full sievert. NASA links that dose to roughly a five percent increase in the risk of a fatal cancer, above the three percent limit it used for astronauts in low Earth orbit.
scenes.headline: A SIEVERT PER MISSION

visual.query: astronaut International Space Station window Earth
visual.note: astronaut looking out a space station window

scenes.narration: That's why many plans have settlers living underground, or under several feet of Martian soil piled over their habitats. The first Martians might rarely see the sky directly. But that's not the strangest thing about Mars. The ground itself has a problem.
scenes.headline: THE FIRST MARTIANS LIVE UNDERGROUND

visual.note: concept art of a Mars habitat shielded by regolith

scenes.narration: Problem five: the dirt. NASA's Phoenix lander found that Martian soil contains salts called perchlorates, at levels of around half a percent, which is considered toxic to humans. And Mars is dusty. Its dust storms can wrap the entire planet and take months to settle.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM FIVE: TOXIC DIRT

visual.note: Phoenix lander's scoop digging into Martian soil

scenes.narration: That dust gets everywhere. Into air locks, seals, suit joints, and eventually lungs. On a planet where your survival depends on machines, fine abrasive dust is a constant enemy. Anything you grow in that soil would first have to be washed clean of those salts.
scenes.headline: DUST GETS EVERYWHERE

visual.note: Mars before and during a planet-wide dust storm

scenes.narration: Problem six: your body. Mars has about thirty-eight percent of Earth's gravity. If you weigh two hundred pounds here, you'd weigh about seventy-six pounds there. That sounds fun, and for a while it would be.
scenes.headline: PROBLEM SIX: YOUR BODY

visual.note: astronaut exercising aboard the space station

scenes.narration: We know that months in zero gravity weaken astronauts' bones and muscles. What we don't know is whether a third of Earth's gravity is enough to keep a body healthy for years, or what it would do to a child growing up there. No one has ever lived in partial gravity long enough to find out.
scenes.headline: A QUESTION NO ONE CAN ANSWER

visual.query: astronauts walking on the Moon Apollo
visual.note: Apollo astronaut walking in low gravity on the Moon

scenes.narration: So that's six ways Mars fights you. Now let's flip it around. What does Mars actually give you to work with? More than you might think. Start with the very thing that makes its air unbreathable.
scenes.headline: NOW FLIP IT AROUND

visual.note: sunset on Mars

scenes.narration: Perseverance carried an experiment called MOXIE that pulled carbon dioxide from the Martian air and split off the oxygen. Over sixteen runs, it made one hundred twenty-two grams of oxygen, about what a small dog breathes in ten hours. Small, but a first: breathable oxygen made on another planet.
scenes.headline: OXYGEN MADE ON MARS

visual.note: MOXIE oxygen experiment being installed in the Perseverance rover

scenes.narration: At its best, MOXIE produced about twelve grams an hour, twice its goal. A full-size version could supply air and, more importantly, the huge amounts of oxygen needed for rocket fuel to fly people home. Making that fuel on Mars, instead of hauling it from Earth, is the difference between a stunt and a settlement.
scenes.headline: FUEL FOR THE TRIP HOME

visual.note: concept art of a rocket lifting off from Mars

scenes.narration: Next, water. Mars has lots of it, frozen. NASA says water ice sits just under the surface in the polar regions, and the northern polar cap is mostly water ice. Melt it, and you have drinking water, water for crops, and, by splitting it, more oxygen.
scenes.headline: WATER, FROZEN

visual.query: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter exposed ice cliff
visual.note: exposed ice in a Martian cliff seen from orbit

scenes.narration: And here's a surprise. In twenty twenty-four, scientists studying marsquakes recorded by NASA's InSight lander concluded that the best explanation was liquid water, deep in cracked rock seven to twelve miles underground. If that's true across the planet, it could be enough to cover Mars in a layer more than half a mile deep.
scenes.headline: AN OCEAN UNDERGROUND?

visual.note: InSight lander's seismometer on the Martian surface

scenes.narration: The catch? Even on Earth, drilling just half a mile is a challenge, and the global estimate assumes one spot represents the whole planet. As one of the researchers put it, drilling that deep on Mars would be extremely difficult. For now, ice near the surface is what settlers would use.
scenes.headline: TOO DEEP TO DRINK

visual.note: map of near-surface ice on Mars

scenes.narration: Put it all together, and here's the honest answer. Could humans live on Mars? Probably, in the sense that people live in Antarctica: in sealed, shielded buildings, making their own air and water, heavily supplied from home, for months or years at a time.
scenes.headline: THE HONEST ANSWER

visual.note: research station in the Antarctic ice

scenes.narration: Living there without help from Earth, raising families, growing all your own food, is a much harder problem, and nobody knows yet how long it would take to solve. It's a frontier, not a backup planet.
scenes.headline: A FRONTIER, NOT A BACKUP

visual.note: Jezero crater delta seen from orbit

scenes.narration: Because here's the strangest comparison of all. Sixty-six million years ago, right after the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs, Earth was dark and freezing. Even on that terrible day, it still had air you could breathe and a magnetic field to protect you. Mars, on its best day, has neither.
scenes.headline: EARTH ON ITS WORST DAY

visual.note: Earth and Mars shown side by side

scenes.narration: None of that means we shouldn't go. It means the first people who walk on Mars will be explorers, carrying their whole world with them. And everything they learn about surviving there will teach us how rare and precious this blue planet really is.
scenes.headline: CARRYING THEIR WORLD WITH THEM
